extracted.intended_audience: comics creators, teachers/students of comics page design, webcomic artists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for choosing, using, and modifying page grids when designing comics pages (print or web), including templates, reading flow, beat-counting, and considerations for web-to-print translation. Includes a hands-on exercise for practicing a nine-panel grid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grids as basic patterns (not rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grids are divisions of the page based on fixed proportions; they are not rules of any kind, just good basic patterns to utilize and use in page design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand you can modify and play with them in many ways (knocking out walls, dutch angles, organic panels), but treat them as reliable starting patterns that save time and help get comics done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability, clarity, and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Grids benefit from being easy to read, clear, and well composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a grid make sure the page reads unambiguously and the composition supports the story; avoid modifications that confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose grid based on story beats and page goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use grid templates as rules of thumb driven by the story beats and what you’re trying to accomplish with the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count your beats and pick a grid that fits the number and rhythm of beats you need on the page. The author suggests using the 4, 6, 9, or 16 as starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorize common grids (4, 6, 9, 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic grid examples to internalize are 4-panel, 6-panel, 9-panel, and 16-panel grids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These serve as reliable starting templates; the author favors the 9-panel as a workhorse but notes uses for each (e.g., 4 and 16 for print-friendly even splits). Use posted page templates with markers for thumbnailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9-panel as a narrative/visual rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: A 3x3 (nine) panel grid often yields pleasing reading rhythms and can echo a three-act story structure; visually it can feel like a 'visual Haiku' or Golden Mean on its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 9 when you want medium-density pages that allow a range to raise or drop beats; you can join cells or knock out walls while keeping the baseline grid intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even-split grids for web-to-print translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Grids that divide evenly along the middle (4, 6, 12, 16) work well for web comics that will be collected for print volumes because online two pages can stack as one in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan with scaling and layout in mind: using even-split grids simplifies handling two-page spreads, keeps a constant aspect ratio, and makes lettering scaling for legibility more manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for lettering legibility and consistent aspect ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing for both web and print, consider how lettering will scale and keep a constant aspect ratio for legibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose grids and page dimensions that make it feasible to set letter sizes that remain readable when pages are displayed online and later printed/stacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain familiar reading flow conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Grids should leverage the familiar text-reading flow (left-to-right, then down) so that reading order remains predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modifying grids (rotating, knocking out walls, unusual layouts), ensure the reader can still follow the intended sequence; some templates explicitly encode nonstandard orders and should be used with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: You may modify grids but respect flow and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: You can modify grids (join panels, use dutch angles, non-rectangular or organic panels, montage/mural layouts), but modifications should serve the story and preserve legibility/flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment freely (round panels, organic gutters, montage) but test reading order and pacing; the author endorses trying basics first and exploring advanced design later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use templates and thumbnailing to speed production
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-made page templates with markers for each grid to make layout and thumbnailing easier so creators can focus on drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print templates for rapid Comic Jam-style work; templates reduce time spent on layout decisions and help maintain consistent page structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count beats and choose a grid that fits beat density
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the narrative beats you want on a page and select a grid that accommodates that number effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nine-panel grid is medium density and flexible; the 16 gives higher density, 4 or 6 gives lower density. Adjust by joining or removing walls to match beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit panel-wall knockouts when practicing
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exercise the student is allowed to knock out as many as three panel walls total when using a nine-panel grid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constraint helps preserve the baseline grid while permitting some variation; in general, limit knockouts so the page remains readable and rhythmically coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select scenes with concise beats and dialogue for tight grids
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pick scenes with long speeches or long continuous scenes for dense grids like nine panels; the material needs to fit into word balloons and the selected number of panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an exercise using nine panels, depict from the scene's first shot to the last using nine moments; pause video to pick moments and keep pencils rough—focus on evocative beats rather than full dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about reading order for nonstandard templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Some templates (e.g., 'Trick 6 Organic') are drawn to read in a specific, possibly non-linear order (left-to-right, down, right-to-left, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or creating such templates, note and design for the intended reading sequence so readers follow the narrative without confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotate/apply grids for different aspect ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Grids intended for print/tablet can be applied on their sides to better suit monitor-favoring aspect ratios common in webcomics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider rotating or adjusting templates to match the target display medium while maintaining beat structure and reading flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use grids to structure space and time in story
rubrics_metrics.description: Grids provide an overt means to structure space and time in your story, aligning panel form with narrative content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing page and panel forms, consider how the layout relates to the story's pacing and temporal structure; different grid choices will shape the reader’s experience of time and rhythm.
